title: Pauri 30, sound: ekaa maaee

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 29: wisdom the meal, and your line, compassion serves the food. Did you hand something over kindly? Today, a new stanza, and it opens like a story. Day two hundred thirteen.

Plenty of languages have a way of starting a story so the listener knows one is coming. Once upon a time. Long, long ago. In the beginning. A child hears those words and settles in, even before anything has happened. The sound itself says: listen, this is how things came to be. Pauri 30 of Japji opens with that kind of sound. Four words, two pairs, and the pairs rhyme, so it lands in the ear like the first line of a very old tale. It's still part of Guru Nanak's answer to the yogis, and it takes a picture they already knew. Today we just hear it.
screen: `ONCE UPON A TIME.` → `A SOUND THAT SAYS, LISTEN.` → `FOUR WORDS, TWO RHYMES.`

segments.voice: Here is how Pauri 30 begins: ekaa maaee jugat viaaee, tin chele paravaan. Start with the first pair. Ekaa: one, a single. Maaee: mother. Ekaa maaee: one mother. Say it, and notice how the two words lean on the long aa sound. Then the second pair. Jugat: a way, a method, and also a joining. Commentators note it was also a yogi word for technique. Viaaee: gave birth, brought forth. So: by a certain joining, she gave birth. Now listen to the rhyme: maaee, viaaee. The line swings like a cradle. Then the next three words: tin chele paravaan. Tin: three. Chele: disciples, students, the same word you'd use for a guru's followers. Paravaan: accepted, approved. One mother, by a joining, brought forth three approved disciples. Who is this one mother? Commentators answer in different ways. Some read her as maya, the power that makes the visible world. Others hear the Creator's own creative power. We'll open that tomorrow, along with who the three are. And at the end of the stanza, the refrain returns in full: aad aneel anaad anaahat, jug jug eko ves. The first, the pure, without beginning, unbroken, one form through every age. You've heard that line close pauris 28 and 29. Notice how it answers today's opening. The story starts with a birth. The refrain reminds you who was never born.
screen: `EKAA MAAEE — ONE MOTHER.` · `JUGAT VIAAEE — BY A JOINING, A BIRTH.` · `TIN CHELE PARAVAAN — THREE DISCIPLES.` · `JUG JUG EKO VES — ONE THROUGH EVERY AGE.` · then, large: `EKAA MAAEE.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly, three times: ekaa maaee jugat viaaee, tin chele paravaan. Let the rhyme rock a little, maaee, viaaee, like something you'd say to a child at night. After the third time, stay quiet. Breathe in, and silently think ekaa, one. Breathe out, and think maaee, mother. Keep that gentle rhythm until the bell. If your mind drifts, the rhyme will bring you back. The bell holds the time.
Chele, disciples, students. It opens like an ancient tale: one mother, by a joining, gave birth to three approved disciples.
Your line: ekaa maaee. Today, think of one person or place you came from, and let the words one mother sit with that thought for a moment. Day two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 30 is one of four stanzas addressed to the Nath yogis, and like the others it closes with the refrain aades tisai aades and aad aneel anaad anaahat, jug jug eko ves.

maaee and viaaee: it swings like a cradle.
every commentator agrees who the one mother is

the refrain says the One was born in the beginning
anaad: without beginning. the story has a birth; the One has none.

fork.setup: a stanza opens: one mother, by a joining, gave birth. what does she bring forth in Pauri 30?
fork.reveal: tin chele paravaan: three approved disciples. tomorrow, who they are and who sees them.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 30: one mother, by a joining, gave birth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about somebody's mother.
what it means: a picture of how creation unfolds: one source bringing forth three powers.
what a scholar hears: some read maaee as maya; jugat can mean both method and union, and commentators note the yogis used it for their techniques.

notes: Gurmukhi quoted in transliteration as the original text; English glosses are paraphrase.
Ang 7 for Pauri 30; confirm (it may begin at the foot of Ang 6).
anaahat glossed as unbroken; it is also often rendered unstruck or indestructible. Confirm preferred gloss.
Two readings of ekaa maaee (maya; the Creator's creative power) presented without ranking; confirm the Keeper is content with the framing.
viaaee glossed as gave birth; some translate as 'conceived' or 'was wed'. Confirm.
